title: Chemical reactions: how vinegar, baking soda and rusting iron make new substances

summary.text: Stir baking soda into water and dry the water away, and the baking soda comes back. Stir baking soda into vinegar, and it fizzes. When that liquid is dried, the white powder left behind is no longer baking soda. A chemical reaction has made new substances. Your child tests this leftover powder and learns five signs of a reaction. They also watch steel wool rust inside an upturned glass, and measure how much of the air the rusting uses.
summary.art: Two small steel pans side by side, each with a white crust inside, and a spoon dropping vinegar on to each: one crust is fizzing and the other is not.

intro.hook: A new iron tawa is grey and hard. Leave it wet for a week, and brown flakes cover it. Nobody painted it. So where did the brown flakes come from?
intro.text: The iron joined with oxygen, a gas in the air, and with water. Together they made a new substance called rust. Rust is brown and crumbly, and iron is neither. A change that makes a new substance is called a chemical reaction. In this unit you make vinegar and baking soda fizz. Then you test whether the baking soda is still there after the fizz. You also find out how much of the air a piece of rusting steel uses up.
intro.art: A grey iron tawa on a kitchen counter with a patch of orange-brown rust where a few drops of water were left on it.

outcomes: I can say what a chemical reaction is, and how it differs from melting, mixing and dissolving.
I can name the reactants and the products when vinegar meets baking soda.
I can name five signs of a chemical reaction, and explain why a sign alone is not proof.
I can test whether a new substance has formed, by checking what the substance does.
I can explain what rust is, what iron needs in order to rust, and how people protect iron.
I can explain that a reaction rearranges atoms, and does not make or destroy them.
I can explain that some reactions give out heat and others take heat in.
I can give examples of chemical reactions in the kitchen, in my body and beyond the Earth.

explanations.concept: A chemical reaction makes new substances
explanations.definition: A chemical reaction is a change in which substances turn into new substances. The new substances have different properties from the ones you started with.
explanations.description: The substances you start with are called reactants. The new substances are called products. A product is not a mixture of the reactants. It is a different substance, and it behaves differently. Iron is hard and grey. Oxygen is a gas you cannot see. When they react with water, the product is rust, which is brown and crumbles between your fingers. Chemists write a reaction as a word equation. The reactants go on the left of an arrow, and the products go on the right. Iron + oxygen + water → rust. The arrow means 'react and make'.
examples: Iron + oxygen + water → rust.
Vinegar + baking soda → carbon dioxide + water + a salt.
Candle wax + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.
Milk turns to curd when bacteria change the milk sugar into an acid.
explanations.art: A word equation drawn with pictures: a nail, a cloud labelled oxygen and a water drop on the left of an arrow, and a heap of brown rust on the right.

explanations.concept: A physical change keeps the same substance
explanations.definition: A physical change is a change in shape, size or state. No new substance is made.
explanations.description: Melting, freezing, boiling, cutting, bending and dissolving are physical changes. Ice, water and steam are one substance in three states. Salt stirred into water seems to vanish, but the salt is still there. If the water dries up, the same salt is left behind, and it still tastes salty. In the After the Fizz experiment you dry two liquids. Baking soda that was only dissolved in water comes back as a powder that still fizzes in vinegar. Baking soda that reacted with vinegar does not come back. That is the difference between a physical change and a chemical reaction.
examples: Wax melts in a warm lamp and sets hard again. It is still wax.
Sugar dissolves in tea. The tea is sweet, so the sugar is still there.
A sheet of paper torn into pieces is still paper.
Water boils into steam, and steam turns back into water on a cool lid.
explanations.art: An ice cube, a puddle and a wisp of steam in a row, all labelled 'water'.

explanations.concept: What the fizz of vinegar and baking soda makes
explanations.definition: Vinegar and baking soda react and make three products: carbon dioxide gas, water and a salt called sodium acetate.
explanations.description: Vinegar is water with a little acetic acid in it, about 4 or 5 parts in every 100. Baking soda is a white powder whose full name is sodium bicarbonate. When the two meet, the acetic acid and the baking soda are used up. The carbon dioxide leaves as bubbles, which is the fizz. The water joins the liquid. The sodium acetate stays dissolved, so you do not see it until the liquid is dried. In the After the Fizz experiment, a white crust is left in the pan. It looks a little like baking soda, but vinegar dropped on it makes no fizz. It is sodium acetate, one of the products. The fizz stops when one reactant runs out. If the baking soda runs out first, more vinegar makes no more bubbles.
examples: Lime juice and cooking soda fizz in the same way, because lime juice is also sour.
Dhokla and bhatura batter rise because soda and sour curd make carbon dioxide inside them.
Fruit salt fizzes in water because it holds baking soda and a dry acid together.
explanations.art: A tumbler of fizzing liquid with three labelled arrows coming out: bubbles labelled carbon dioxide, a drop labelled water and a few crystals labelled sodium acetate.

explanations.concept: Five signs of a reaction, and why a sign is only a clue
explanations.definition: A sign of a reaction is something you can notice that suggests a new substance may be forming.
explanations.description: There are five common signs. One, a gas appears, as bubbles or a fizz. Two, the colour changes. Three, a new solid appears in a liquid. Four, the mixture gets warmer or cooler without any stove or ice. Five, light or a new smell is given off. In the Six Mixes, Five Signs activity you look for these. But a sign can mislead. Water bubbles when it boils, and no new substance is made. Tea goes paler when you add plain water, and that is only mixing. Salt seems to disappear in water, and that is only dissolving. So a sign is a clue. To be sure, you test what the substance does afterwards. Does it still behave like the old substance, or does it behave differently?
examples: Gas: lime juice fizzes on baking soda.
Colour: black tea turns much paler when lime juice goes in.
New solid: warm milk makes white lumps when lime juice goes in.
Heat and light: a sparkler at Deepavali glows and gets very hot.
explanations.art: Five numbered pictures in a row: a fizzing cup, a cup of tea in two shades, a cup of milk with white lumps, a hand feeling a cool tumbler and a glowing sparkler.

explanations.concept: Rusting: iron reacts with oxygen and water
explanations.definition: Rusting is a slow chemical reaction. Iron, oxygen and water react and make rust.
explanations.description: Iron needs both oxygen and water to rust. Dry iron in dry air stays grey for years. Salt in the water makes rusting faster, so iron rusts quickly near the sea. Steel is mostly iron, so ordinary steel rusts too. Rust takes up more room than the iron it came from. So rust swells, cracks and flakes off, and fresh iron underneath is open to the air again. This is why a rusting gate can be eaten right through. In the Rust Uses Up Air experiment, wet steel wool rusts inside an upturned glass. The water climbs into the glass, because the rusting takes oxygen out of the air inside. People protect iron by keeping oxygen and water away from it. Paint and oil cover it. Galvanising covers it with zinc. Stainless steel has the metal chromium mixed in. The chromium reacts with oxygen and makes a very thin, clear skin, which keeps more oxygen out.
examples: A window grill near the sea at Kochi or Visakhapatnam rusts faster than one in dry Jaipur.
An iron kadai is rubbed with oil after washing, to keep water and air off it.
A galvanised bucket stays grey for years, even though it is wet every day.
A stainless steel tumbler does not rust in the kitchen.
explanations.art: A cut-away drawing of a painted iron bar with a scratch in the paint, a water drop on the scratch and a patch of rust swelling up under the paint.

explanations.concept: A reaction rearranges atoms. It does not make or destroy them
explanations.definition: In a chemical reaction, the atoms of the reactants come apart and join up in new groups. Every atom that goes in comes out.
explanations.description: Everything is made of atoms, and there are about 90 kinds in nature. Each kind is called an element. Iron, oxygen, hydrogen and gold are elements. In a reaction the atoms change partners. Two hydrogen molecules and one oxygen molecule have six atoms. They rearrange into two water molecules, which also have six atoms. You do this with coins and seeds in the Atom Swap activity. Because no atom is lost, the products weigh exactly as much as the reactants. A fizzing bowl gets lighter only because its gas floats away. If the gas is caught, nothing is lost. A reaction also cannot change one kind of atom into another. No reaction can turn iron atoms or lead atoms into gold atoms.
examples: Hydrogen + oxygen → water. Six atoms go in and the same six come out.
A bowl of vinegar and baking soda weighs a little less after the fizz, because carbon dioxide has left.
Rust weighs more than the iron did, because oxygen atoms from the air have joined it.
explanations.art: Two pairs of small balls and one pair of large balls on the left of an arrow, and on the right two groups, each of one large ball joined to two small balls.

explanations.concept: A new substance behaves unlike the substances that made it
explanations.definition: The properties of a product are its own. They are not a blend of the properties of the reactants.
explanations.description: When you mix lime juice and sugar, the drink is sour and sweet. A mixture keeps the properties of its parts. A reaction is different. Sodium is a soft metal that catches fire in water. Chlorine is a green, poisonous gas. When they react, the product is the salt you sprinkle on your food. Hydrogen is a gas that burns, and oxygen is the gas that flames need. Joined together they make water, which puts fires out. The atoms are the same atoms as before. What changed is which atoms are joined to which. So what a substance does depends on how its atoms are joined. Chemists have recorded more than 200 million different substances, all made from the same few kinds of atoms.
examples: Sodium + chlorine → table salt.
Hydrogen + oxygen → water.
Hard grey iron + invisible oxygen + water → crumbly brown rust.
Sour vinegar + baking soda → a gas, water and a salt that does not fizz.
explanations.art: A piece of silvery metal and a jar of green gas on the left of an arrow, and a small bowl of white table salt on the right.

explanations.concept: Reactions give out heat or take heat in
explanations.definition: Every chemical reaction either gives out energy or takes energy in. We usually notice this as heat.
explanations.description: Burning gives out a lot of heat and light, very fast. Rusting gives out heat too, but so slowly that you do not notice. Some hand-warmer packets hold iron powder, salt and water. When the packet is opened to the air, the iron rusts quickly and the packet stays warm for hours. Other reactions take heat in from whatever is around them. Vinegar and baking soda do this. In the Cold Fizz activity, one tumbler of vinegar fizzes with baking soda. It ends up a few degrees cooler than a tumbler of plain vinegar. A leaf making sugar takes in energy too, as light from the Sun.
examples: A burning candle gives out heat and light.
Your body stays warm because reactions in your cells give out heat.
A fizz of vinegar and baking soda takes in heat and feels cool.
A leaf takes in sunlight to make sugar from carbon dioxide and water.
explanations.art: Two steel tumblers side by side, one fizzing with a small blue arrow pointing in and one still, with a child's hands reaching for both.

explanations.concept: Living bodies run on chemical reactions
explanations.definition: Every living body is kept going by chemical reactions, thousands of different kinds at the same time.
explanations.description: When you eat rice, reactions in your mouth and gut break the starch into sugar. In your cells, sugar reacts with the oxygen you breathe in. The products are carbon dioxide and water. The reaction gives out the energy you use to move, think and keep warm. You breathe the carbon dioxide out. A green leaf runs the opposite reaction. With energy from sunlight, the leaf makes sugar and oxygen from carbon dioxide and water. Bacteria run reactions too. Curd bacteria change milk sugar into an acid, and the acid makes the milk set. Humans and other animals, plants and bacteria all stay alive by keeping their reactions going.
examples: Sugar + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water, in your cells.
Carbon dioxide + water → sugar + oxygen, in a leaf in sunlight.
Idli batter rises overnight because tiny living beings in the batter make carbon dioxide.
explanations.art: A child breathing out beside a potted tulsi in sunlight, with a small arrow labelled carbon dioxide going from the child to the leaves and one labelled oxygen coming back.

explanations.concept: Reactions on the Earth and far beyond it
explanations.definition: Chemical reactions happen wherever atoms can meet: in rocks, in the sea, in the air and in space.
explanations.description: Mars looks red from the Earth because the dust on Mars is full of iron that has joined with oxygen. In a way, Mars is a rusty planet. On the Earth, most iron is found in the ground as iron ore, which is iron already joined with oxygen. Steel plants at Bhilai, Visakhapatnam and Jamshedpur run a reaction that takes the oxygen away and leaves iron. Reactions also happen in the cold clouds of gas and dust between the stars. Astronomers have found more than 200 kinds of molecules there, including water. The fastest part of any reaction is the moment when atoms let go and join again. It takes less than a millionth of a millionth of a second. The Egyptian-born chemist Ahmed Zewail found a way to watch this moment with very short flashes of laser light. He won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1999.
examples: The red dust of Mars is iron joined with oxygen.
Iron ore + carbon, heated very strongly → iron + carbon dioxide.
Water molecules have been found in clouds of gas between the stars.
explanations.art: The red planet Mars in a dark sky, with a small inset picture of a rusty nail lying on red-brown dust.

agreed.text: A chemical reaction makes new substances, with properties different from those of the reactants.
agreed.evidence: Chemists test what substances do before and after a change. The products melt, dissolve, burn and react in different ways from the reactants.

agreed.text: A reaction rearranges atoms and loses none of them, so the total weight stays the same.
agreed.evidence: In the 1770s and 1780s, Antoine Lavoisier ran reactions in sealed glass vessels and weighed them before and after. The weight did not change.

agreed.text: Rust is iron joined with oxygen and water, and iron needs both in order to rust.
agreed.evidence: Iron kept in dry air, or under boiled water sealed with oil, stays grey. Iron in open water or damp air rusts.

agreed.text: About one fifth of the air is oxygen.
agreed.evidence: When iron rusts or a fuel burns in a closed space, about one fifth of the air is used up. Careful measurements give 21 parts of oxygen in every 100 parts of air.

agreed.text: The gas made by vinegar and baking soda is carbon dioxide.
agreed.evidence: The gas is heavier than air, puts out a flame and turns clear limewater milky. The Scottish chemist Joseph Black studied this gas in the 1750s.

agreed.text: No chemical reaction can change one element into another.
agreed.evidence: Alchemists tried for about two thousand years to make gold from other metals, and none did. We now know that a reaction only changes how atoms are joined.

challenging.claim: A chemical change can never be undone.
challenging.for: Burnt paper cannot be unburnt, and a boiled egg cannot be made raw again.
challenging.against: Many reactions can be reversed by another reaction. Tea made pale by lime juice goes dark again with baking soda. Steel plants turn iron ore, which is like rust, back into iron. A phone battery runs its reactions backwards each time it is charged.

challenging.claim: Bubbles always mean that a chemical reaction is happening.
challenging.for: Vinegar and baking soda bubble, and that is a reaction.
challenging.against: Boiling water bubbles, and a bottle of soda bubbles when it is opened. In both cases no new substance is made. A sign is a clue, and only a test of the substance can settle it.

challenging.claim: Dissolving salt in water is a chemical change, not only a physical one.
challenging.for: When salt dissolves, its crystals break up into tiny charged particles, and water molecules crowd round each one. The salty water carries electricity, which dry salt and pure water hardly do.
challenging.against: Most school books call dissolving a physical change, because the same salt comes back when the water dries. Both sides agree on what happens. They disagree about which name fits best.

challenging.claim: Rust weighs less than the iron it came from, because the iron is being eaten away.
challenging.for: A rusty gate looks thinner and weaker, and bits fall off it.
challenging.against: If all the rust is collected, it weighs more than the iron did. The extra weight is oxygen and water that have joined the iron.

challenging.claim: The right chemical reaction could turn lead into gold.
challenging.who: Alchemists in many countries, for about two thousand years.
challenging.for: Reactions do change substances completely. A grey metal can become a red powder, so gold did not seem impossible.
challenging.against: A reaction only changes how atoms are joined. It cannot change lead atoms into gold atoms. Around 1980, scientists did change a tiny amount of the metal bismuth into gold. They did it by smashing atoms in a giant machine, which is not a chemical reaction. It cost far more than the gold was worth.

big_questions.q: Baking soda fizzes away in vinegar. Every one of its atoms is still in the pan or the air. Is the baking soda still there?
big_questions.hint: Think about a word and its letters. If you rearrange the letters, is the word still there?

big_questions.q: Bubbles, colour and warmth can all mislead. How can anyone be sure that a new substance has formed?
big_questions.hint: In the After the Fizz experiment, you dropped vinegar on a white crust to see whether it fizzed.

big_questions.q: Hydrogen is not wet and oxygen is not wet. Where does the wetness of water come from?
big_questions.hint: Is wetness inside the atoms, or does it belong to the way they are joined?

big_questions.q: Iron is made from a rusty-looking rock called iron ore. When iron rusts, is something being spoiled or being returned?
big_questions.hint: A person who owns the gate and the ground the ore came from might answer differently.

big_questions.q: Chemists can make substances that never existed before, such as plastics. Who should decide which new substances are made?
big_questions.hint: A new substance can be useful for fifty years and stay in the sea for five hundred.

big_questions.q: Your body is made from food, water and air that have reacted. Is there anything in you that was not in them?
big_questions.hint: Rust is brown, and neither iron nor oxygen is brown.

story.title: The Lamp Went Down First
story.note: Devika, Ammamma, Sheeba chechi and their well are made up. These things are real. Carbon dioxide is about one and a half times as heavy as air. It collects in old wells, pits and tanks where leaves and other things rot. People have long lowered a flame to test for it. Stirring the air with leafy branches is an old method. Lifting the gas out with a bucket is Devika's idea in the story, and it works only slowly. The lamp test is not a safety rule. A well can hold other dangerous gases, or too little oxygen, even where a flame still burns. Trained workers today use gas meters and blowers. Children should never lean over a well or go into a well, pit or tank.
text: The well behind Ammamma's house was older than the house. Its wall was built of red laterite stone, and small ferns grew out of the cracks.

For two years nobody had drawn water from it. Ammamma had been living with Devika's family in Kochi, and the house near Thrissur had stayed locked. Now it was the April holidays. They had come back, and the well had to be cleaned before anyone drank from it.

Sheeba chechi came at seven in the morning with a coir rope, two buckets and a bamboo ladder. She cleaned wells all over the village. She looked down at the dark water, and at the thick mat of jackfruit leaves floating on it.
"Two years of leaves," she said. "This will take until lunch."

Devika, who was nine, stood back from the wall, where Ammamma had told her to stand. From there she could still see down the well. The air inside it looked like any other air. She could see straight through it to the leaves.
Sheeba chechi tied the rope round her waist and swung one leg over the wall.
"Wait," said Ammamma. "The lamp goes down first."

She had brought a small clay lamp from the kitchen, with oil and a cotton wick. She lit it, stood it in a bucket and let the rope out slowly. Devika watched the flame go down, steady and yellow. Half way to the water it shrank to a blue bead. Then it went out.
"Wind," said Sheeba chechi.
"There is no wind in a well," said Ammamma. She pulled the bucket up, lit the lamp and lowered it again. At the same depth, the flame went out again.
Sheeba chechi took her leg back over the wall. Nobody spoke.
Devika stared into the well. Nothing had touched the flame. Nothing was there. Then she remembered the evening before.

The power had gone off at dusk. Ammamma had been stirring a pinch of cooking soda into lime juice, because her stomach felt heavy after the journey. The tumbler frothed and hissed beside the lamp on the table. Devika had picked the tumbler up to look, and tipped it a little towards the flame. Not one drop spilled. But the flame bent, shrank and went out.
"What did I do?" she had asked.

"You poured something on it," Ammamma had said, lighting the lamp again. "When soda meets something sour, the two of them make a new gas. You cannot see it. It is heavier than air, so it sits in the tumbler the way water does. And a flame goes out in it."
Now Devika looked from the well to her grandmother. "Ammamma, is it the same gas down there?"

"The same," said Ammamma. "Leaves do not just lie there. They rot, and rotting is a slow change. It makes that same heavy gas, a little every day. In an open field the wind carries it off. In a well it has nowhere to go. For two years it has been filling this well from the bottom."
"A person who climbs into it cannot tell," said Sheeba chechi quietly. "It has no colour and no smell. A man I know went down a well like this, in Palakkad. They pulled him out just in time."
Devika thought of the tumbler again. The gas had stayed in it like water. It had poured like water.
"If it sits there like water," she said slowly, "can we lift it out like water? With the bucket?"

Sheeba chechi laughed, and then she stopped laughing. "We usually stir it out," she said. "We tie leafy branches to a rope and pull them up and down, so that fresh air mixes in. But a bucket will carry some up as well. We will do both."

So for an hour they worked. Sheeba chechi lowered the empty bucket to the water and drew it up gently. Each time she carried it to the edge of the yard and tipped out what looked like nothing at all. Devika and Ammamma pulled a bundle of mango branches up and down on the second rope until their arms ached. A crow watched from the jackfruit tree while three people worked hard at emptying an empty well.
Then Ammamma lit the lamp once more and let it down. The flame passed the half-way mark. It went on down, small and yellow, until it stood just above the leaves. It stayed lit.

Sheeba chechi kept the lamp burning in a bucket beside her all the time she worked, and the rope stayed round her waist. Ammamma held the other end and watched the flame. By lunch the leaves lay in a wet heap in the yard, and the water at the bottom showed a round piece of sky.
That evening Devika squeezed half a lime into a tumbler and added a pinch of soda. She watched the froth rise and settle. Above the liquid, the tumbler looked empty. She knew now that it was not.
story.epiphany: The gas at the bottom of the well looked exactly like air. So did the gas above the fizzing lime juice. Devika could tell each one from air only by what it did to a flame. A reaction makes a new substance, and you know a new substance by how it behaves.
ask: Why could nobody see that the air in the well had changed?
The leaves in the well were not burning or fizzing. How could they make a gas?
How would you tell two clear liquids apart without tasting them?
