rules: A family is three cards: two reactants and the product they make. The answer key shows all eight families.
Shuffle the cards. Deal five cards to each player. Put the rest face down in a pile, and turn the top card face up beside it.
On your turn, take one card. Take either the top card of the pile or the face-up card.
If you hold a whole family, lay it down and read it aloud as a word equation. For example, say 'iron plus oxygen and water make rust'.
The other players check the family against the answer key. A wrong family goes back into your hand.
End your turn by putting one card face up on the face-up card. Two cards that name the same substance can stand in for each other.
The game ends when the pile runs out. The player with the most families wins.
Playing alone? Spread all 24 cards face up and sort them into eight families. Time yourself, then check with the answer key. Play again to beat your time.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and the answer key. Spread the cards face up. Read three or four of them aloud together.
flow.say: Each card names one substance. A reactant is a substance that goes into a reaction. A product is a new substance that comes out.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Spread them face up. Read a few aloud.
flow.context: This is the first step of Reaction Families. You cut out the cards and read what is on them.

flow.do: With the cards still face up, your child tries to build all eight families before looking at the answer key. Then check each family against the key.
flow.say: Try to put each product with the two reactants that make it. Guess first. We will check with the answer key afterwards.
flow.kid: Put each product with its two reactants. Then check the key.

ask.q: Which product looks least like the reactants that made it?
good: Table salt, because sodium burns and chlorine is poisonous.
Water, because hydrogen and oxygen are both gases.
Rust, because iron is hard and rust crumbles.

flow.parent: This sorting round teaches the families. Do not worry about mistakes here. Two cards say Oxygen and two say Water, and either one may be used in either family.
flow.context: In this step of Reaction Families you sort the face-up cards into eight families. Then you check them with the answer key.

flow.do: Shuffle and deal five cards each. Play by the rules until the pile runs out. Each family that is laid down must be read aloud as a word equation.
flow.say: Now we play. Draw one card, lay down a family if you have one, and put one card back. Read every family aloud.
flow.kid: Draw a card. Lay down a family if you can. Put one card back.
flow.parent: A child playing alone sorts all 24 cards against a timer, and then tries to beat that time.
flow.context: In this step of Reaction Families you play the card game and read each family aloud as a word equation.

flow.do: Count the families. Then look at the eight product cards together and ask the question below.
flow.say: Look at the eight products. Is any product simply a mixture that looks like both of its reactants?
flow.kid: Count your families. Does any product look like its reactants?

check.q: Sodium burns in water and chlorine is a poisonous gas. What do they make together?
options: Table salt, which is safe to eat
check.why: They make table salt. A product has its own properties. If you chose 'a poisonous metal that burns', you were thinking of a mixture. A mixture keeps the properties of its parts.

flow.context: This is the last step of Reaction Families. You count your families and compare each product with its reactants.

experiments.title: After the Fizz: is the baking soda still there?
experiments.question: Baking soda stirred into water dissolves. Baking soda stirred into vinegar fizzes. If both liquids are dried, does baking soda come back from each one?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. When the two liquids are dried, what will be left in each pan? Will each leftover still fizz when vinegar is dropped on it? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same amount of baking soda in both tumblers. Do this by making four equal heaps from one level teaspoon. Use the same amount of liquid in both: 2 tablespoons and 1 teaspoon. Dry both liquids in the same kind of pan, on the same low flame. Let both pans cool before the drop test, because a hot pan makes any liquid sizzle. Drop the same 5 drops of vinegar on each leftover. Only one thing differs: one tumbler has water and the other has vinegar.
results_table: What was left in the pan
Did it fizz when 5 drops of vinegar were added?

materials.item: baking soda, also called cooking soda (not baking powder): 1 level teaspoon
white vinegar: about 4 tablespoons (or strained lime juice if you have no vinegar)
drinking water: 2 tablespoons and 1 teaspoon
steel tumblers, labelled W for water and V for vinegar
small steel pans, such as tadka pans. One pan washed and used twice also works
a tablespoon, a teaspoon, a butter knife and a dry steel plate
a gas stove, used by the grown-up only
the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up does all the heating. Hot vinegar gives off a sharp smell, so open a window and keep faces away from the pan. Salt-like crusts can spit when they are nearly dry, so use a low flame and stand back. Let the pans cool before anyone touches them. Nobody tastes anything in this experiment.
experiments.record: Fill in the results table with one row for the water pan and one row for the vinegar pan. Add a third row for fresh baking soda. Then write one sentence that begins 'After the fizz, the baking soda was…'.
experiments.context: In this experiment you dissolve baking soda in water and react baking soda with vinegar. You dry both liquids and test whether baking soda comes back from each.

setup.art: A level teaspoon of white powder tipped on to a steel plate and divided with a butter knife into four small equal heaps.
setup.caption: 1. Divide 1 level teaspoon of baking soda into 4 equal heaps.

setup.art: Two steel tumblers labelled W and V, one with clear still liquid and one with fizzing liquid, each with a small heap of powder being tipped in.
setup.caption: 2. Put one heap in water and one heap in vinegar. Wait for the fizz to end.

setup.art: A grown-up holding a small steel pan over a low gas flame, with a thin layer of liquid steaming in it.
setup.caption: 3. A grown-up dries each liquid in a pan on a low flame.

setup.art: Two cooled steel pans, each with a white crust on the bottom, and a child dropping vinegar from a teaspoon on to one crust.
setup.caption: 4. Let the pans cool. Drop 5 drops of vinegar on each crust.

setup.art: A notebook table with three rows and the words 'fizzed' and 'no fizz' written in the last column.
setup.caption: 5. Write what was left, and whether it fizzed.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: A white crust, a little glassy

flow.do: Show your child the baking soda, the water and the vinegar. Explain what you will do. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both down.
flow.say: We will stir baking soda into water, and the same amount into vinegar. Then we will dry both liquids. What will be left in each pan? Will each leftover still fizz in vinegar? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One heap goes in water. One goes in vinegar. What will be left after drying? Why?

good: The powder is still in the water, so it will come back.
The fizz used the powder up, so nothing will be left.
Something will be left, but I do not know what.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children expect baking soda to come back from both, and some expect an empty pan after the fizz.
flow.context: This is the first step of After the Fizz. You guess what will be left when each liquid is dried.

flow.do: Tip 1 level teaspoon of baking soda on to the dry plate. Divide it into 4 equal heaps with the knife. Put 2 tablespoons of water in tumbler W and 2 tablespoons of vinegar in tumbler V. Tip one heap into each tumbler and stir.
flow.say: Make four heaps of the same size. One heap goes into the water and one into the vinegar. Watch both tumblers. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Make four equal heaps. Tip one into water and one into vinegar. Watch.

check.q: Why must both tumblers get the same amount of baking soda?
options: So only the liquid is different
check.why: A fair test changes one thing. Here the one thing is the liquid. If you chose 'so both tumblers fizz', remember that water and baking soda do not fizz at all.

flow.parent: Keep the two spare heaps on the plate. One is for the drop test later. Do the stirring on a tray, because the vinegar tumbler froths up.
flow.context: In this step of After the Fizz you put equal heaps of baking soda into water and into vinegar.

flow.do: When the fizz in tumbler V has stopped, add 1 more teaspoon of vinegar and watch. If it fizzes again, wait and add another teaspoon. Add 1 teaspoon of water to tumbler W for each teaspoon of vinegar.
flow.say: Has the fizz stopped? Add one more teaspoon of vinegar. If there are no new bubbles, the baking soda has all reacted.
flow.kid: Add one more teaspoon of vinegar. Are there new bubbles?
flow.parent: This step makes sure no baking soda is left over. With most vinegars, the first extra teaspoon gives no bubbles. Lime juice varies, so it may need two or three.
flow.context: In this step of After the Fizz you check that the fizz has finished, by adding a little more vinegar.

flow.do: Open a window. Pour tumbler W into one pan and heat it on a low flame until the liquid has just gone. Take it off the stove. Do the same with tumbler V in the second pan. Stand both pans where they can cool.
flow.say: I will dry each liquid on the stove. Stand back and watch from there. Tell me what you see appear as the water goes.
flow.kid: A grown-up dries both liquids. Stand back. Watch what appears in each pan.
flow.parent: Each pan takes about 3 to 4 minutes. Take the pan off while a small wet patch is left. The heat of the pan finishes the job. The vinegar pan smells sharp. If you prefer no stove, pour each liquid into a wide steel plate and leave it under a fan. It dries in about a day, or two days in the rains.
flow.context: In this step of After the Fizz a grown-up dries the water mixture and the vinegar mixture in two pans.

flow.do: Wait until both pans are cool enough to hold. Look closely at the two crusts together. Scrape a little of each with the knife.
flow.say: Both pans have something white in them. Do the two crusts look the same? Can you tell by looking which one is baking soda?
flow.kid: Look at both white crusts. Do they look the same?
flow.parent: The pans must be cool. A drop of any liquid sizzles on a hot pan, and that would look like a fizz. The crust from the vinegar pan is often a little glassy or flaky.
flow.context: In this step of After the Fizz you compare the white crusts left in the two cooled pans.

flow.do: Drop 5 drops of vinegar on a spare heap of fresh baking soda. Then drop 5 drops on the crust in pan W, and 5 drops on the crust in pan V. Record each result.
flow.say: First, see what fresh baking soda does with five drops of vinegar. Now try the crust from the water pan. Now try the crust from the vinegar pan.
flow.kid: Drop vinegar on fresh baking soda. Then on each crust. Which ones fizz?

check.q: A white crust does not fizz when vinegar is dropped on it. What does that tell you?
options: It is very old baking soda
check.why: Baking soda always fizzes in vinegar. A powder that does not fizz is a different substance. If you chose 'the vinegar has run out', remember that the same vinegar made the fresh heap fizz.

flow.parent: In most homes the fresh heap and the water crust fizz at once. The vinegar crust only gets wet and starts to dissolve. If the vinegar crust fizzes a little, some baking soda was left over. That means step 3 needed more vinegar.
flow.context: In this step of After the Fizz you drop vinegar on fresh baking soda, and then on each crust.

flow.do: Look at the results table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Where is the baking soda that went into the vinegar?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Baking soda came back from the water. Why did it not come back from the vinegar?
good: It reacted with the vinegar and became something new.
The fizz used it up.
It turned into the gas and the new crust.

ask.q: Both crusts are white. How did you tell them apart?
good: By what they did with vinegar.
One fizzed and one did not.

flow.parent: The reason: in water, baking soda only dissolves, so the same substance is left when the water goes. In vinegar, baking soda reacts with the acid. The products are carbon dioxide gas, water and a salt called sodium acetate. The gas left as bubbles, and the sodium acetate is the crust. The dried water crust may be partly changed by the heat into washing soda, which also fizzes.
flow.think: The bubbles floated away. How could you find out what gas they were made of?
flow.context: This is the last step of After the Fizz. You say what the drop test showed about the two white crusts.

experiments.title: Rust Uses Up Air: how far will the water climb?
experiments.question: Wet steel wool is left to rust inside an upturned glass that stands in water. Does the water climb into the glass? If it does, how far does it climb before it stops?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will the water inside the glass with steel wool go up, go down or stay where it is? How far will it move in three days? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use two glass tumblers of the same size and shape. Push a wad of wet steel wool into the bottom of one glass. Push a wad of wet tissue paper of the same size into the other. Stand both upside down in the same depth of water, side by side, away from sunlight. Mark both water levels at the start, and measure both at the same time each day. Only one thing differs: one glass has iron in it.
results_table: Glass with steel wool: how many centimetres the water has climbed
Glass with wet tissue: how many centimetres the water has climbed
What the steel wool looks like

materials.item: clear glass tumblers of the same size, with straight sides if possible
fine steel wool, the iron kind from a hardware or paint shop: a wad the size of a lime. A shiny stainless steel kitchen scrubber will not work
white vinegar: half a cup, to clean the steel wool
tissue paper or cotton: a wad the size of a lime
deep steel plates or flat bowls
coins, two under the rim of each glass
strips of sticking tape or rubber bands, to mark the water levels
a ruler, a pencil and the results table

schedule.what: Guess. Set up the two upturned glasses and mark the water levels.
Measure how far the water has climbed in each glass. Look at the steel wool.
Measure again. Work out what share of the air was used. Explain the result.

experiments.record: Fill in one row of the results table each day. On day 3, draw the glass with steel wool and mark the starting level and the last level.
experiments.context: In this experiment wet steel wool rusts inside an upturned glass that stands in water. You measure how far the water climbs into the glass over three days.

setup.art: A wad of grey steel wool being pushed with a pencil into the bottom of a clear glass tumbler, with a bowl of vinegar beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Dip the steel wool in vinegar, squeeze it, and push it into the bottom of one glass.

setup.art: Two glass tumblers standing upside down in plates of water, each resting on two coins, one with grey steel wool at the top and one with white tissue.
setup.caption: 2. Stand both glasses upside down in water, on two coins each.

setup.art: A close view of an upturned glass with a strip of tape marking the water level inside it and a ruler held beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Mark the water level inside each glass with tape.

setup.art: The same two glasses two days later: the steel wool is orange-brown and the water inside its glass stands about a fifth of the way up, while the other glass is unchanged.
setup.caption: 4. Each day, measure how far the water has climbed.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results, for glasses with 10 centimetres of air

flow.do: Day 1. Show your child the steel wool and the two glasses. Explain the set-up. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both down.
flow.say: We will leave wet steel wool inside an upturned glass that stands in water. Will the water inside the glass go up, go down or stay? How far will it move in three days? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Wet steel wool sits in an upturned glass. Will the water inside move? Why?

ask.q: What is inside the glass, besides the steel wool?
good: Air.
Air, and a little water at the bottom.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Some children expect no change, because the glass 'has nothing in it'.
flow.context: This is the first step of Rust Uses Up Air. You guess what the water inside the upturned glass will do.

flow.do: Soak the steel wool in the vinegar for 1 minute. Squeeze it out and pull it loose. Push it into the bottom of one glass so that it stays there when the glass is turned over. Wet the tissue with water and push it into the other glass.
flow.say: The vinegar cleans the thin coat off the steel, so that rusting can start. Push the wad right to the bottom. It must not fall out.
flow.kid: Dip the steel wool in vinegar. Squeeze it. Push it into the glass.
flow.parent: Pull the wad loose so that air can reach all of it. If steel wool pricks the fingers, use a spoon or wear a kitchen glove. Wash hands afterwards.
flow.context: In this step of Rust Uses Up Air you put wet steel wool in one glass. You put wet tissue in the other.

flow.do: Pour water 2 centimetres deep into each plate. Put two coins in each plate. Stand each glass upside down with its rim on the coins. Mark the water level inside each glass with tape. Measure from the tape to the top of the air space and write it down.
flow.say: The coins let water pass under the rim. Mark where the water stands inside each glass now. How tall is the air space above the mark?
flow.kid: Stand both glasses upside down in water. Mark the water level with tape.

check.q: Why is there a second glass, with wet tissue and no steel wool?
options: To show what happens without iron
To make the water climb faster
To keep the first glass steady
check.why: The second glass is the comparison. If its water stays put, then the climb in the first glass was caused by the steel wool. If you chose 'to make the water climb faster', remember that the two glasses do not touch.

flow.parent: Keep the glasses out of direct sun, where they will not be knocked. Top up the plates if the water gets low. The rims must stay under water all the time.
flow.context: In this step of Rust Uses Up Air you stand both glasses upside down in water. Then you mark the starting levels.

flow.do: Day 2. At about the same time of day, measure from the tape up to the new water level inside each glass. Record both. Look at the colour of the steel wool.
flow.say: Has the water moved in either glass? Measure from the tape to the water. What has happened to the steel wool?
flow.kid: Measure from the tape to the water in each glass. Look at the steel wool.
flow.wait: Do this one day after setting up
flow.parent: With steel wool cleaned in vinegar, the water has usually climbed 1 centimetre or more by now. If nothing has moved, check that the wool is the iron kind and that it is still damp.
flow.context: In this step of Rust Uses Up Air you measure both water levels one day after setting up.

flow.do: Day 3. Measure and record both levels again. Compare the climb with the height of the air space you wrote down on day 1.
flow.say: Measure again. How far has the water climbed in all? Is that more or less than half of the air space?
flow.kid: Measure both glasses again. How far has the water climbed in all?
flow.wait: Do this two days after setting up
flow.parent: The water usually stops after climbing about one fifth of the air space. In a glass with 10 centimetres of air that is about 2 centimetres. Anything from 1.5 to 2.5 centimetres is a good result. If the water is still climbing, measure once more tomorrow.
flow.context: In this step of Rust Uses Up Air you measure both water levels two days after setting up.

flow.do: Look at the results table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Why did the water stop climbing, when there is still steel wool left?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: What took up the space that the water moved into?
good: Air that got used up.
The part of the air that joined the iron.
Oxygen.

ask.q: Why did the water in the tissue glass stay where it was?
good: There was no iron to rust.
Nothing used up the air in that glass.

flow.parent: The reason: rusting is a reaction between iron, oxygen and water. The steel wool took oxygen out of the air in the glass, and the oxygen became part of the rust. Water moved up to fill the space. About one fifth of the air is oxygen. When the oxygen had gone, the rusting stopped, although iron was left. The rest of the air is mostly nitrogen, which does not react with iron.
flow.think: What would happen if you lifted the glass for a moment, let fresh air in and set it down again?
flow.context: This is the last step of Rust Uses Up Air. You say why the water climbed into the glass with steel wool and then stopped.

activities.title: Six Mixes, Five Signs: which mixes make something new?

materials.item: small cups or katoris, numbered 1 to 6
baking soda (cooking soda): 2 level teaspoons
limes or lemons, squeezed and strained, to give 6 teaspoons of juice
salt: 1 teaspoon
black tea with no milk, cooled: half a cup
warm milk, as warm as a hot drink: 4 tablespoons
water, a tablespoon, a teaspoon, a tray and the signs table

schedule.what: Make six mixes one at a time. Look for the five signs. Decide which mixes made a new substance.

activities.record: A table with six rows, one for each mix. Write what you mixed, which sign you saw, and your decision: 'new substance' or 'same substances'.
activities.context: In this activity you make six kitchen mixes, one at a time. You look for five signs of a reaction and decide which mixes made a new substance.

setup.art: Six small steel katoris in a row on a tray, numbered 1 to 6, with a lime, a jar of baking soda, salt, a cup of black tea and a cup of milk behind them.
setup.caption: 1. Number six cups. Set out the baking soda, lime juice, salt, tea, milk and water.

setup.art: A child tipping a teaspoon of lime juice on to white powder in a katori, with froth rising.
setup.caption: 2. Make one mix at a time. Watch closely for one minute.

setup.art: A notebook table with six rows and columns headed 'What I mixed', 'Sign I saw' and 'New substance?'.
setup.caption: 3. Write the sign you saw. Decide: new substance, or the same substances?

flow.do: Set out the six cups and the ingredients on a tray. Write the five signs at the top of the table. They are: a gas appears, the colour changes, a new solid appears, the mix warms or cools, light or a new smell.
flow.say: A sign is a clue that a new substance may be forming. There are five common signs. We will make six mixes and hunt for them. Nobody tastes anything.
flow.kid: Set out six cups. Learn the five signs. Do not taste anything.
flow.context: This is the first step of Six Mixes, Five Signs. You set out six cups and learn the five signs of a reaction.

flow.do: Mix 1: 1 teaspoon of baking soda and 2 teaspoons of lime juice. Mix 2: 1 teaspoon of salt stirred into 4 tablespoons of water. Mix 3: 1 teaspoon of baking soda stirred into 4 tablespoons of water. Before each mix, ask for a guess. After each, record the sign.
flow.say: Before each mix, tell me what you think will happen. Then mix, watch for a minute, and tell me which sign you saw, if any.
flow.kid: Make mixes 1, 2 and 3. Guess first. Which signs do you see?

ask.q: The salt has disappeared. Is that one of the five signs?
good: No, disappearing is not on the list.
No. The salt is still there, because the water would taste salty.

flow.parent: Mix 1 fizzes at once. Mixes 2 and 3 show no sign: the powders only dissolve. A little baking soda may stay at the bottom of mix 3.
flow.context: In this step of Six Mixes, Five Signs you make three mixes with baking soda, lime juice, salt and water.

flow.do: Mix 4: 4 tablespoons of black tea and 2 teaspoons of lime juice. Mix 5: 4 tablespoons of black tea and 2 teaspoons of water. Mix 6: 4 tablespoons of warm milk and 2 teaspoons of lime juice. Hold cups 4 and 5 side by side against white paper.
flow.say: Guess first each time. Compare the two cups of tea. Did both change colour by the same amount? Now watch the milk for one minute.
flow.kid: Make mixes 4, 5 and 6. Compare the two teas. Watch the milk.
flow.parent: The tea with lime juice turns much paler, from dark brown to orange. The tea with water hardly changes. The warm milk makes small white lumps in a thin, watery liquid. Cold milk does this more slowly.
flow.context: In this step of Six Mixes, Five Signs you add lime juice to tea and to warm milk. You add plain water to a second cup of tea.

flow.do: Look at the table together. For each mix, your child decides: new substance, or the same substances? Then ask the questions below.
flow.say: Which mixes do you think made something new? Which ones only mixed or dissolved? How sure are you about each one?
flow.kid: Decide for each mix. Is there a new substance, or the same ones?

ask.q: Mix 5 went a tiny bit paler. Why is that not a reaction?
good: The water only spread the tea out.
It is the same tea, with more water in it.

ask.q: How could you check whether the baking soda in mix 3 is still baking soda?
good: Dry it and see if the powder still fizzes.
Add lime juice and see if it fizzes.

check.q: Which of these is a sign of a reaction?
options: Bubbles appear when two things are mixed
Tea gets paler when water is added
check.why: A gas that appears on mixing is one of the five signs. Salt in water has only dissolved, and tea with more water has only been spread out. If you chose one of those, ask whether the same substance is still there.

flow.parent: Mixes 1, 4 and 6 are reactions. Mixes 2, 3 and 5 are not. A sign is only a clue. In the After the Fizz experiment, you check by drying a liquid and testing the powder that is left.
flow.context: This is the last step of Six Mixes, Five Signs. You decide which of the six mixes made a new substance.

activities.title: Cold Fizz: can your hands feel a reaction?

materials.item: steel tumblers of the same size, each holding at least 300 millilitres
white vinegar: 200 millilitres, which is about 1 cup
baking soda: 2 level teaspoons
a tray or a large steel plate, to catch froth
a cloth to cover the eyes, a teaspoon and a pencil

schedule.what: Make a fizz in one of two tumblers of vinegar. Then find the cooler tumbler with your eyes covered.

activities.record: Write four lines, one for each try. Put a tick if you picked the fizz tumbler as the cooler one, and a cross if you did not.
activities.context: In this activity you make a fizz in one of two tumblers of vinegar. Then you test, with your eyes covered, whether your hands can tell which tumbler got cooler.

setup.art: Two steel tumblers on a tray, each half full of clear vinegar, with a jar of baking soda and a teaspoon beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Pour the same amount of vinegar into two steel tumblers.

setup.art: One of the two tumblers frothing up as a teaspoon of white powder goes in, while the other stays still.
setup.caption: 2. Add 2 teaspoons of baking soda to one tumbler, a little at a time.

setup.art: A child with a cloth over her eyes holding one steel tumbler in each hand.
setup.caption: 3. With eyes covered, hold both. Which one feels cooler?

flow.do: Pour 100 millilitres of vinegar into each tumbler, which is about half a cup. Stand both on the tray for 2 minutes. Your child holds one in each hand and says whether they feel the same.
flow.say: Both tumblers hold the same vinegar from the same bottle. Hold one in each hand. Do they feel equally cool? When one fizzes, will it get warmer, get cooler or stay the same? Why?
flow.kid: Hold both tumblers. Do they feel the same? What will the fizz do?
flow.parent: Any guess with a reason is fine. Many children expect a fizz to be warm, because it looks like boiling.
flow.context: This is the first step of Cold Fizz. You check that two tumblers of vinegar feel the same, and guess what a fizz will do.

flow.do: Add 2 level teaspoons of baking soda to one tumbler, half a teaspoon at a time, and stir. Stir the other tumbler too. Wait 1 minute for the froth to settle.
flow.say: Add the baking soda slowly, so the froth stays in the tumbler. Stir the plain one as well, so both are treated alike.
flow.kid: Add baking soda to one tumbler, slowly. Stir both. Wait one minute.
flow.parent: The froth rises fast, so keep the tumblers on the tray. Wipe any spilled liquid off the outside of the tumblers before the next step.
flow.context: In this step of Cold Fizz you add baking soda to one of the two tumblers of vinegar.

flow.do: Cover your child's eyes. Swap the tumblers round, or leave them, without saying which. Put one in each of their hands. They say which hand holds the cooler one. Do this 4 times and record each answer.
flow.say: Eyes covered. I am putting one tumbler in each hand. Which hand holds the cooler one? Take your time.
flow.kid: Cover your eyes. Hold both tumblers. Which hand has the cooler one?
flow.parent: The fizz tumbler is usually 3 to 5 degrees cooler, which most hands can tell. Do the four tries quickly, because the tumblers slowly warm up again. If you have a kitchen thermometer, measure both. Do not use a fever thermometer.
flow.context: In this step of Cold Fizz you find the cooler tumbler four times with your eyes covered.

flow.do: Count the ticks. Ask your child what they found, and where the coolness came from. Then explain, using the note below.
flow.say: How many times out of four did you pick the fizz tumbler? Nobody added ice. So why is it cooler?
flow.kid: Count your ticks. Nobody added ice. Why is one tumbler cooler?

ask.q: Which of the five signs of a reaction did you just feel?
good: The mix got cooler by itself.
A change in warmth.

flow.parent: The reaction of vinegar and baking soda takes in heat. It takes the heat from the liquid and the tumbler, so they cool down. Burning does the opposite and gives heat out. If both tumblers felt the same every time, say so plainly. The difference is small and some hands miss it.
flow.context: This is the last step of Cold Fizz. You count how often you found the cooler tumbler, and ask why the fizz made it cool.

activities.title: Atom Swap: make water and rust without losing an atom

materials.item: coins of one kind, to stand for iron atoms
rajma or other dark seeds, to stand for oxygen atoms
white chana, groundnuts or other pale seeds, to stand for hydrogen atoms
a sheet of paper with a line down the middle, headed 'Before' and 'After'
a pencil

schedule.what: Build the reactants from seeds and coins. Rearrange them into the products. Count the atoms before and after.

activities.record: For each reaction, write the number of each kind of atom before and after. Draw the groups you made.
activities.context: In this activity coins and seeds stand for atoms. You build the reactants, rearrange them into the products, and count the atoms before and after.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a line down the middle headed Before and After, and on the Before side two pairs of pale seeds and one pair of dark seeds.
setup.caption: 1. On the 'Before' side, build two hydrogen molecules and one oxygen molecule.

setup.art: The same seeds moved to the After side and regrouped as two groups, each made of one dark seed and two pale seeds.
setup.caption: 2. Move the same seeds across and regroup them as two water molecules.

setup.art: Four coins and three pairs of dark seeds on the Before side, and on the After side two groups, each of two coins and three dark seeds.
setup.caption: 3. Do the same for rust: 4 iron atoms and 6 oxygen atoms.

flow.do: On the 'Before' side, make two pairs of pale seeds and one pair of rajma. Explain that each pair is a molecule. Your child counts the atoms of each kind and writes the numbers.
flow.say: A pale seed is a hydrogen atom. A rajma is an oxygen atom. Hydrogen gas is made of pairs, and so is oxygen gas. How many atoms of each kind are on the table?
flow.kid: Make two pairs of pale seeds and one pair of rajma. Count them.
flow.context: This is the first step of Atom Swap. You build hydrogen and oxygen molecules from seeds and count the atoms.

flow.do: Your child moves the same seeds to the 'After' side and makes water molecules. Each water molecule is one rajma with two pale seeds. No seed may be added or left behind. Count again.
flow.say: A water molecule is one oxygen atom with two hydrogen atoms. Use only the seeds you have. How many water molecules can you make? Are any seeds left over?
flow.kid: Move the seeds across. Make water: one rajma with two pale seeds.

check.q: Two hydrogen molecules and one oxygen molecule react. How many atoms are there afterwards?
options: Two, one for each water molecule
check.why: There were 4 hydrogen atoms and 2 oxygen atoms, which is 6. A reaction only regroups them, so there are still 6. If you chose 3 or 2, you counted the groups and not the atoms.

flow.parent: The seeds make exactly two water molecules, with nothing left over. Four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms go in, and the same six come out.
flow.context: In this step of Atom Swap you rearrange the hydrogen and oxygen seeds into two water molecules.

flow.do: Clear the paper. On the 'Before' side put 4 coins, each on its own, and 3 pairs of rajma. Your child regroups them on the 'After' side into rust: each group has 2 coins and 3 rajma. Count before and after.
flow.say: A coin is an iron atom. Rust is made of groups of two iron atoms with three oxygen atoms. How many groups can you make? Is anything left over?
flow.kid: Put down 4 coins and 6 rajma. Make groups of 2 coins and 3 rajma.
flow.parent: This makes exactly two groups. It is a simple picture of rust. Real rust also holds some water.
flow.context: In this step of Atom Swap you rearrange coins and rajma into two groups that stand for rust.

flow.do: Put 4 coins and only 1 pair of rajma on the 'Before' side. Ask how much rust can be made now. Then ask the questions below.
flow.say: Now there are four iron atoms and only two oxygen atoms. Can you finish even one group of rust? What would you need more of?
flow.kid: Try with 4 coins and only 2 rajma. Can you finish one group?

ask.q: Could you make a gold atom by regrouping these coins and seeds?
good: No, there is no gold atom on the table.
No. Regrouping cannot make a new kind of atom.

ask.q: What happens to a reaction when one reactant runs out?
good: It stops.
The other reactant is left over.

flow.parent: With two oxygen atoms, no group of rust can be finished, because each group needs three. The reaction stops when a reactant runs out. In the Rust Uses Up Air experiment, the rusting stops when the oxygen in the glass is used up. Steel wool is still left.
flow.context: This is the last step of Atom Swap. You find out what happens when there are too few oxygen atoms to make rust.

projects.title: The Rust Survey: ten iron things and how each one is protected

materials.item: a notebook page with a table of ten rows
a pencil, and coloured pencils for the rust map
a fridge magnet, to check which things are iron or steel

schedule.what: Find ten things made of iron or steel at home. Record where each one is, how it is protected and whether it has rust.
Sort the ten things. Find the pattern. Draw a rust map of your home.

projects.record: A table with ten rows and four columns: the thing, where it is kept (dry, sometimes wet, or outdoors), how it is protected (paint, oil, zinc coat, stainless steel or nothing), and whether you can see rust.
projects.context: In this two-day project you find ten iron or steel things in your home. You record how each one is protected from rust, and look for a pattern.

setup.art: A child holding a fridge magnet against a painted window grill, with a notebook under her arm.
setup.caption: 1. Find ten things of iron or steel. A magnet sticks to most of them.

setup.art: A close view of a scratched patch on a painted iron gate, with rust showing in the scratch and a pencil pointing at it.
setup.caption: 2. Look closely. How is each thing protected? Is there rust?

setup.art: A hand-drawn plan of a flat with small orange dots marked at the balcony grill, the bathroom window and the kitchen sink.
setup.caption: 3. Draw a plan of your home. Mark every place where you found rust.

flow.do: Day 1. Walk through your home together. Find ten things of iron or steel. Look at window grills, gates, a tawa, scissors, buckets, taps, a cycle, a cupboard, a lock and steel tumblers. For each one, fill in the four columns.
flow.say: For each thing, tell me three things. Is it kept dry, or does it get wet? What covers the metal? Can you see any rust? Before we start, where do you expect to find the most rust?
flow.kid: Find ten iron or steel things. Is each one wet or dry? Covered? Rusty?
flow.parent: Rust often shows where paint is chipped, at joints and screws, and low down where water collects. Do not touch flaking rust with a cut finger, and wash hands afterwards. A magnet does not stick to some stainless steel, so count kitchen tumblers anyway.
flow.context: This is day 1 of The Rust Survey. You find ten iron or steel things at home and record how each is protected.

flow.do: Day 2. Sort the ten things into two lists: rust seen, and no rust seen. Look for what the rusty things share.
flow.say: Look at the rusty list. What do those things have in common? Now look at the list with no rust. What kept the oxygen and water away from them?
flow.kid: Make two lists: rust and no rust. What do the rusty things share?
flow.wait: Do this the day after the survey

ask.q: Why is there rust where the paint has chipped?
good: Air and water can reach the iron there.
The paint was keeping oxygen and water out.

flow.context: This is day 2 of The Rust Survey. You sort your ten things into rusty and not rusty, and look for a pattern.

flow.do: Draw a simple plan of your home. Mark an orange dot wherever you found rust. Talk about the question below.
flow.say: Where are most of the dots? Which rooms are the wettest? If you could protect one thing better, which would it be, and how?
flow.kid: Draw your home. Mark the rust with orange dots. Where are most dots?
flow.parent: Most homes find the dots at balconies, bathrooms and near the sink. In towns by the sea there are usually more, because salt speeds up rusting.
flow.context: This is the last step of The Rust Survey. You draw a rust map of your home and say where iron rusts most.

challenges.title: The Self-Filling Bag: firm in 30 seconds, with no burst
challenges.problem: A car's airbag fills in less than a tenth of a second. A chemical reaction inside the airbag makes the gas. Your problem is a slower one. Make a sealed bag fill itself with gas from vinegar and baking soda. The bag must be firm within 30 seconds of mixing, and it must not pop open.
constraints: Use only vinegar and baking soda to make the gas.
The bag must be sealed before the two reactants meet.
The bag must be firm within 30 seconds, and stay shut.
Work over a tray or in the sink, and keep faces away from the bag.
materials: 3 small zip pouches, about 15 centimetres by 20 centimetres, or thin clear polythene bags with rubber bands
tissue paper, cut into squares the size of your palm
a tablespoon, a teaspoon and a quarter-teaspoon measure if you have one
a tray or the kitchen sink, and a cloth for spills
a clock or phone that shows seconds
general: Fold the baking soda into a square of tissue. Drop the packet into the vinegar, and seal the bag before the tissue soaks through.
Start with small amounts, such as a quarter teaspoon of baking soda and 2 tablespoons of vinegar, and build up.
Change only one amount at a time, and write down every recipe and its result.
creative: Hold the powder in one corner of the bag with a rubber band on the outside. Seal the bag, then pull the band off.
Put the vinegar in a small inner pouch that opens when the outer bag is squeezed.
Warm the vinegar tumbler in a bowl of warm water first, so that the gas is made faster.
challenges.your_turn: Write your best recipe on a card, so clearly that someone else can follow it. Then take a bag of a different size. Work out the amounts before you test, and see how close you get.
challenges.context: In this challenge you make a sealed bag fill itself with carbon dioxide from vinegar and baking soda. You must find the amounts that make it firm but do not pop it open.

setup.art: A small zip pouch on a tray with two tablespoons of clear vinegar in the bottom, and a child holding a folded tissue packet above it.
setup.caption: 1. Put vinegar in the bag. Fold baking soda into a tissue packet.

setup.art: The zip pouch sealed shut with the tissue packet inside, bubbles rising round the packet and the bag beginning to swell.
setup.caption: 2. Drop the packet in, seal the bag fast and shake it once.

setup.art: Three zip pouches in a row on a tray: one limp, one firm like a small pillow and one that has popped open with froth spilling out.
setup.caption: 3. Too little, just right or too much? Change one amount and try again.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Do a first test over the tray: 2 tablespoons of vinegar in the bag, a quarter teaspoon of baking soda in a tissue packet. Drop it in, seal, shake once and watch for 30 seconds.
flow.say: This first recipe is small on purpose. Watch what the bag does in thirty seconds. Is it firm, or limp?
flow.kid: Try the small recipe first. Seal the bag. Watch for 30 seconds.

ask.q: The bag is limp. Which reactant would you add more of, and why?
good: More baking soda, because it all got used up.
Both, because more reactants make more gas.

flow.parent: This small recipe leaves the bag only about a third full. Make sure the zip is fully closed. A leaking zip is the usual reason for a bag that never fills.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Self-Filling Bag. You test a small recipe of vinegar and baking soda in a sealed bag.

flow.do: Your child chooses a new recipe and writes it down before testing. Rinse the bag, or take a fresh one, and test it. Record: limp, firm or popped.
flow.say: Choose your next recipe and write it down first. Change only one amount. Then test it and write what happened.
flow.kid: Write a new recipe. Change one amount. Test it. Write what happened.
flow.parent: Half a teaspoon of baking soda with 3 tablespoons of vinegar usually makes this size of bag firm. A whole teaspoon with 6 tablespoons usually pops the zip, so do that one in the sink.
flow.context: In this step of The Self-Filling Bag you change one amount in your recipe and test again.

flow.do: Test once more to improve the result. Then double only the baking soda and keep the vinegar the same. See whether the bag gets any fuller.
flow.say: Now double the baking soda, and keep the vinegar the same. Before you test, will the bag be twice as full? Why?
flow.kid: Double only the baking soda. Will the bag get twice as full?

ask.q: The bag did not get fuller, and white powder was left. Why?
good: The vinegar ran out.
There was not enough vinegar for the extra baking soda.

flow.parent: When the vinegar runs out, extra baking soda makes no extra gas. In the Atom Swap activity, coins were left over when the rajma ran out. This is the same idea.
flow.context: In this step of The Self-Filling Bag you double the baking soda and find out whether the bag gets fuller.

flow.do: Your child writes the best recipe on a card. Talk about the question below.
flow.say: Write your best recipe so that a stranger could follow it. An airbag must fill to exactly the right size. How do you think its makers decide how much reactant to put in?
flow.kid: Write your best recipe on a card. Could a stranger follow it?
flow.parent: Praise a clear record of what failed as much as a firm bag. Rinse the bags and the sink with plenty of water afterwards.
flow.context: This is the last step of The Self-Filling Bag. You write down the recipe that made the bag firm without popping.

worksheets.title: New substance, or the same substance?

items.p: What is a chemical reaction?
opts: A change that makes new substances
A change of shape or size
items.why: A chemical reaction turns substances into new substances with different properties. Bubbles and heat can also come with changes that make nothing new, such as boiling.

items.p: When ice melts, a new substance is made.
items.why: False. Ice and water are the same substance in two states. Melting is a physical change, and the water can freeze again.

items.p: The substances that go into a chemical reaction are called ____.
items.why: Reactants go in and are used up. Vinegar and baking soda are the reactants in a fizz.

items.p: A new substance made by a chemical reaction is called a ____.
items.why: Products come out of a reaction. Rust is the product when iron, oxygen and water react.

items.p: Sort these changes. Does each one make a new substance, or keep the same substance?
items.why: Rusting, curdling and burning are chemical reactions, and their products behave differently. Melting, dissolving and tearing change only the state, the mixing or the shape.

items.p: Match each sign of a reaction to an example.
pairs: Lime juice fizzes on baking soda
Black tea turns pale with lime juice
Warm milk makes white lumps with lime juice
Vinegar cools as baking soda fizzes in it
items.why: These are the five common signs. Each one is a clue that a new substance may be forming.

items.p: Which gas is in the bubbles when vinegar meets baking soda?
items.why: The bubbles are carbon dioxide, one of the three products. If you chose steam, remember that nothing was heated.

items.p: Which two things does iron need in order to rust?
items.why: Rust forms when iron reacts with oxygen and water. Salt makes rusting faster, but iron rusts without it.

items.p: Boiling water bubbles, so boiling is a chemical reaction.
items.why: False. The bubbles in boiling water are water that has turned into a gas. No new substance is made. Bubbles are only a clue.

items.p: Put the steps of the After the Fizz experiment in order.
items: Divide the baking soda into equal heaps
Stir one heap into water and one into vinegar
Wait for the fizz to end
a: Divide the baking soda into equal heaps
Stir one heap into water and one into vinegar
Wait for the fizz to end
items.why: Equal heaps make the test fair. The pans must cool before the drop test, because any liquid sizzles on a hot pan.

items.p: In After the Fizz, the crust from the vinegar pan did not fizz in vinegar. Explain what that shows.
items.a: Baking soda always fizzes in vinegar. The crust did not fizz, so it is not baking soda. The baking soda reacted with the vinegar and became a new substance.
items.why: A strong answer uses the test result as evidence, and says that a new substance was made.

items.p: Explain why an iron kadai is rubbed with oil after it is washed.
items.a: Iron rusts when oxygen and water reach it. The oil covers the iron and keeps water and air off it. So the kadai does not rust.
items.why: A strong answer names both oxygen and water, and says that the oil keeps them away from the iron.

items.p: Draw two hydrogen molecules and one oxygen molecule turning into two water molecules. Count the atoms on each side.
items.a: On the left, two pairs of small circles and one pair of large circles. On the right, two groups, each with one large circle and two small circles. Both sides are labelled '6 atoms'.
items.why: A strong drawing uses the same atoms on both sides. There are 4 hydrogen atoms and 2 oxygen atoms before and after.
items.art: A blank box divided by an arrow, with 'Before' written on the left and 'After' on the right.

items.p: A tumbler of vinegar gets cooler when baking soda fizzes in it. Why?
opts: Baking soda is kept in the fridge
items.why: This reaction takes heat in from the liquid and the tumbler, so they cool down. Burning does the opposite and gives heat out.

items.p: Complete the word equation: iron + oxygen + water → ____.
items.why: Rust is the product. It is brown and crumbly, unlike the hard grey iron.

items.p: Three of these are chemical reactions. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Sugar in tea has only dissolved. The tea tastes sweet, so the sugar is still there. The other three make new substances.

items.p: Salt seems to disappear in water. How could you show that the salt is still there?
opts: Let the water dry and look for salt
items.why: When the water dries, the same salt is left behind. That shows the salt only dissolved, and no new substance was made.

items.p: A product always looks and behaves like a blend of its reactants.
items.why: False. A product has its own properties. Sodium burns in water and chlorine is poisonous, yet together they make table salt.

items.p: Tea goes a little paler when plain water is added. Explain why this is not a chemical reaction.
items.a: The water only spreads the tea out, so there is less tea in each spoonful. No new substance is made. If the extra water dried up, the tea would be as dark as before.
items.why: A strong answer says that the same substances are still there, only more spread out.

items.p: In the Rust Uses Up Air experiment, why did water climb into the glass with steel wool?
opts: The steel wool soaked up the water
Rusting used up oxygen in the glass
The coins pushed the water up
items.why: The iron took oxygen out of the air in the glass to make rust. Water moved up into the space the oxygen had filled.

items.p: A glass holds 15 centimetres of air. Rusting uses one fifth. How many centimetres does the water climb?
items.why: One fifth of 15 is 15 divided by 5, which is 3. About one fifth of the air is oxygen, and rusting uses the oxygen.

items.p: Sort these. Does each one protect iron from rust, or help iron to rust?
items.why: Paint, oil and zinc keep oxygen and water off the iron. A chip, a puddle and salty air let them reach it, or speed the reaction up.

items.p: Put these in order, to show how an iron gate rusts under chipped paint.
items: A chip of paint falls off
Air and rain reach the iron
The swelling rust lifts off more paint
a: A chip of paint falls off
Air and rain reach the iron
The swelling rust lifts off more paint
items.why: Rust takes up more room than iron, so it pushes the paint off around the chip. That is why a small chip grows into a large rusty patch.

items.p: Rust weighs more than the iron it came from. Explain where the extra weight comes from.
items.a: When iron rusts, oxygen atoms from the air and some water join the iron. These have weight. So the rust weighs as much as the iron plus the oxygen and water that joined it.
items.why: A strong answer says that something was added to the iron, and names oxygen.

items.p: Which pair of substances reacts to make table salt?
items.why: Sodium is a soft metal and chlorine is a green gas. Their product, table salt, is unlike both of them.

items.p: A chemical reaction can change iron atoms into gold atoms.
items.why: False. A reaction only changes how atoms are joined. Iron atoms stay iron atoms, whatever they join with.

items.p: A town beside the sea must choose the railings for a new footbridge.

views.says: Use stainless steel. It costs about three times as much, but it will not need painting.
Use ordinary steel and paint it. It is cheap now, and we can repaint it every three years.

views.who: A painter who repaints the town's railings
views.says: Painted steel gives people like me steady work. But if the town skips one repainting, the sea air will rust it through.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason, using what you know about rust. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. One reason is that salty air speeds up rusting, so paint by the sea fails sooner. Another is that paint works only while it has no chips.
items.why: Each view has something right in it. A strong answer uses what iron needs in order to rust, and takes the cost and the work seriously.

items.p: Label this picture from the Rust Uses Up Air experiment: the steel wool, the air space and the climbed water.
a: The steel wool: the orange-brown wad at the top of the upturned glass
The air space: between the steel wool and the water
The water that has climbed: between the tape mark and the new water level
items.why: The water climbed from the tape mark into the space where oxygen used to be. The rest of the air space is mostly nitrogen.
items.art: An upturned glass standing on two coins in a plate of water, with a rusty wad at the top, a strip of tape on the side and the water inside standing above the tape, with three blank label lines.

items.p: A bowl of vinegar and baking soda weighs less after the fizz. Does this mean that atoms were destroyed? Explain.
items.a: No. The carbon dioxide gas floated out of the bowl and took its weight with it. If the gas were caught and weighed too, the total would be the same as before.
items.why: A strong answer says where the missing weight went, and that no atom was lost.

items.p: Which of these changes gives out heat?
opts: A leaf making sugar in sunlight
items.why: Burning gives out heat and light. The fizz takes heat in, and a leaf takes light in. Melting ice takes heat in too, and is not a reaction at all.

items.p: Four iron atoms and six oxygen atoms react to make rust. How many atoms are in the rust?
items.why: 4 and 6 make 10. A reaction regroups atoms and loses none. If you chose two, you counted the groups of rust and not the atoms.

items.p: A rust group has 2 iron and 3 oxygen atoms. How many groups do 10 iron and 12 oxygen make?
items.why: 12 oxygen atoms make 4 groups, because 12 divided by 3 is 4. Those groups use 8 iron atoms. The oxygen runs out first, and 2 iron atoms are left over.

items.p: A reaction stops, although plenty of one reactant is left. Give a reason, with an example from this unit.
items.a: The other reactant has run out. In the Rust Uses Up Air experiment, the rusting stopped when the oxygen in the glass was used up. Steel wool was still left.
items.why: A strong answer says that a reaction needs all of its reactants. It gives the steel wool or the leftover baking soda as an example.

items.p: Water is made from hydrogen and oxygen, so water burns as hydrogen does.
items.why: False. Water is a new substance with its own properties. It puts fires out, although hydrogen burns and oxygen helps things to burn.

items.p: Two clear liquids are mixed, and nothing can be seen to change. What can you say?
opts: A reaction may or may not have happened
items.why: Some reactions show no sign that eyes can see. To find out, you would test what the mixture does. Signs are clues, and their absence is not proof either.

items.p: A white powder has no label. Without tasting, how could you test whether the powder is baking soda?
items.a: Put a little of the powder on a plate and drop vinegar or lime juice on it. Baking soda fizzes at once. To be sure, do the same with powder that is known to be baking soda and compare.
items.why: A strong answer tests what the powder does, and compares it with known baking soda. Salt, sugar and flour do not fizz.

items.p: A reaction that takes in heat makes the things around it ____.
items.why: The heat comes out of the things nearby, so they cool down. In the Cold Fizz activity, the tumbler of fizzing vinegar cooled for this reason.

items.p: Match each reaction to the place where it happens.
pairs: In the cells of your body
In a green leaf in sunlight
items.why: The same kinds of reaction happen in living bodies, in factories and on other planets. A leaf runs the reverse of the reaction in your cells.

items.p: Salt is stirred into water until it can no longer be seen. Chemists describe this change in different ways.

views.says: This is a physical change. Dry the water, and the same salt comes back.
This is a chemical change. The salt breaks into charged particles, and the water now carries electricity.
People made the words physical and chemical. Some changes sit between the two.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then say what one of the other views gets right.
items.a: Any view with a reason. One reason is that the salt comes back unchanged. Another is that salty water does something that neither dry salt nor pure water does.
items.why: Working chemists hold each of these views. A strong answer uses evidence, such as what comes back on drying, and is fair to another view.

items.p: Why is no gold made when lead is heated with other substances?
opts: The fire is never hot enough
Gold is too heavy to make
Reactions cannot change one atom into another
items.why: A reaction only regroups atoms. Lead atoms stay lead atoms. Alchemists tried for about two thousand years and never made gold.

items.p: Every chemical reaction either gives out energy or takes energy in.
items.why: True. Burning and rusting give out heat. The fizz of vinegar and baking soda takes heat in, and a leaf takes in light.

items.p: Draw the atoms before and after iron rusts. Show how iron atoms and oxygen atoms are joined afterwards.
items.a: Before: iron atoms packed together, and oxygen atoms in pairs nearby. After: groups in which iron atoms and oxygen atoms are joined to each other. The number of each kind of atom is the same in both pictures.
items.why: A strong drawing keeps every atom, and shows that the change is in which atoms are joined.
items.art: A blank box divided in two, with 'Before rusting' written on the left and 'After rusting' on the right.

items.p: In Rust Uses Up Air, the water climbed one fifth of the air space and stopped. What does this show?
items.a: Only about one fifth of the air can react with iron. That part is oxygen. The other four fifths must be something else, which does not join with iron.
items.why: A strong answer says that air is a mixture, and that only its oxygen was used. The rest is mostly nitrogen.

items.p: Put these changes in order, from the fastest to the slowest.
items.why: An airbag fills in less than a second and a fizz lasts under a minute. Curd takes some hours, and a gate takes years to rust through.

items.p: Tea made pale by lime juice goes dark again when baking soda is added. What does this show?
opts: The lime juice has dried up
Baking soda is a brown dye
Another reaction can reverse some chemical changes
items.why: The lime juice changed the colouring substances in the tea, and the baking soda changed them back. Not every chemical change is permanent.

quiz.p: Which change makes a new substance?
quiz.why: Curd bacteria change milk sugar into an acid, and the milk sets. Freezing, dissolving and cutting make nothing new.

quiz.p: In a word equation, what does the arrow mean?
quiz.why: The reactants are on the left and the products on the right. The arrow says that the reactants react and make the products.

quiz.p: Vinegar and baking soda react. Which list gives the products?
opts: Carbon dioxide, water and a salt
quiz.why: The gas is carbon dioxide. Water and a salt called sodium acetate stay behind in the liquid.

quiz.p: Which of these is not a sign of a reaction?
opts: The mix warms up by itself
quiz.why: Dissolving makes no new substance, and the solid comes back when the liquid dries. The other three are signs.

quiz.p: A fizzy drink bubbles when the bottle is opened. Why is this not proof of a reaction?
opts: The gas was already dissolved in the drink
The drink is too cold to react
quiz.why: The gas was pushed into the drink at the factory and comes out when the cap is opened. No new substance is made, so bubbles alone prove nothing.

quiz.p: What is the surest way to tell that a new substance has formed?
quiz.why: Two substances can look the same, like the two white crusts in After the Fizz. Only a test of what each one does can tell them apart.
Rust is the product when iron reacts with oxygen and water. It is a new substance, and it is no longer iron metal.

quiz.p: Why does a coat of zinc stop a steel bucket from rusting?
opts: It soaks up all the rust
It keeps oxygen and water off the iron
quiz.why: Iron rusts only where oxygen and water reach it. The zinc coat covers the iron. This is called galvanising.

quiz.p: Six atoms go into a chemical reaction. How many atoms come out?
quiz.why: A reaction regroups atoms. It does not make or destroy any, so six go in and six come out.

quiz.p: Why does an open bowl get lighter while vinegar and baking soda fizz in it?
opts: Carbon dioxide gas leaves the bowl
The vinegar dries up at once
quiz.why: The gas has weight, and it floats away. No atom is destroyed. If the gas were caught, the total weight would stay the same.

quiz.p: Which reaction takes heat in, so that the mixture feels cooler?
opts: Iron powder rusting in a hand warmer
Sugar reacting with oxygen in your cells
quiz.why: The fizz of vinegar and baking soda takes heat in. The other three give heat out.

quiz.p: Which reaction happens inside the cells of your body?
opts: Sugar and oxygen make carbon dioxide and water
quiz.why: Your cells react sugar with the oxygen you breathe in. The reaction gives the energy you use to move, think and keep warm.

applications: Cooks use the fizz. Soda and sour curd make carbon dioxide inside dhokla and bhatura batter, and the gas makes them rise.
Steel plants at Bhilai, Visakhapatnam and Jamshedpur turn iron ore into iron. They run a reaction that takes the oxygen away from the iron.
Buckets, roof sheets and electricity pylons are galvanised. A coat of zinc keeps oxygen and water off the steel.
A car's airbag is filled by a chemical reaction. It makes a bagful of gas in less than a tenth of a second.
Fertiliser factories react nitrogen from the air with hydrogen. Crops fed with this fertiliser grow food for about half the people on Earth.
A phone battery gives electricity from a chemical reaction. Charging the phone runs the reaction backwards, ready for next time.
Cement does not simply dry. It reacts with water and turns into a new, hard substance, which is why fresh concrete is kept wet.

open_questions.q: How did the chemical reactions of life first get started on the young Earth?
open_questions.why_open: Every living cell runs thousands of linked reactions. Nobody has yet shown how the first such set began from simple substances.

open_questions.q: Did reactions in space supply some of the ingredients for life?
open_questions.why_open: Rock brought back from the asteroids Ryugu and Bennu contains amino acids, which living bodies use. Scientists do not know how much of this material reached the early Earth.

open_questions.q: Can chemists work out everything a new substance will do before anyone makes it?
open_questions.why_open: For small molecules, computers can now calculate some properties. For large ones, such as a new medicine, the only sure way is to make the substance and test it.

open_questions.q: Can carbon dioxide from the air be turned into fuel or stone cheaply enough to matter?
open_questions.why_open: Plants do it with sunlight, and some factories do it on a small scale. So far the reactions people use need a lot of energy and money.

open_questions.q: Can a coat be made that mends its own scratches, so that steel never rusts?
open_questions.why_open: Chemists are testing paints that release a repairing substance when they crack. None has yet lasted for many years outdoors.

maths.problem: In the Rust Uses Up Air experiment, a glass starts with 10 centimetres of air. The water climbs 2 centimetres and stops. What fraction of the air was used up?
maths.explain: 2 centimetres out of 10 centimetres is 2 tenths. Divide the top and the bottom by 2, and 2 tenths becomes 1 fifth. So about one fifth of the air is oxygen.
maths.context: In the Rust Uses Up Air experiment, wet steel wool rusts inside an upturned glass. Water climbs into the glass as the oxygen is used.
maths.why_maths: A fraction turns one glass's result into a fact about air that is true for a glass of any size.

maths.problem: A tall jar holds 25 centimetres of air above wet steel wool. Rusting uses one fifth of the air. How far should the water climb? After a week it has climbed only 3 centimetres. Give one possible reason.
maths.answer: It should climb 5 centimetres. One possible reason is that the steel wool dried out and stopped rusting early.
maths.explain: One fifth of 25 is 25 divided by 5, which is 5 centimetres. A climb of 3 centimetres means some oxygen is still in the jar. The steel wool may have dried out, or it may be too tightly packed for air to reach it.
maths.context: In the Rust Uses Up Air experiment, the water climbs about one fifth of the way up the air space. Here the idea is used on a taller jar.
maths.why_maths: A prediction made from a fraction lets you notice when a result is odd, and then look for the cause.

maths.problem: In the Atom Swap activity, one water molecule needs 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom. You have 14 pale seeds for hydrogen and 9 rajma for oxygen. How many water molecules can you make, and what is left over?
maths.answer: 7 water molecules, with 2 rajma left over.
maths.explain: 14 divided by 2 is 7, so the pale seeds are enough for 7 molecules. Those 7 molecules use 7 rajma. 9 take away 7 is 2, so 2 oxygen atoms are left over.
maths.context: In the Atom Swap activity, seeds stand for atoms. You regroup them from reactants into products without adding or losing any.
maths.why_maths: Dividing shows which reactant runs out first, and that tells you how much product a reaction can make.

maths.problem: These are made-up numbers. A bowl of vinegar weighs 180 grams. 5 grams of baking soda are stirred in. After the fizz, the bowl weighs 183 grams. How many grams of gas left the bowl? What would a sealed bag of the same mixture weigh after the fizz?
maths.answer: 2 grams of gas left the bowl. The sealed bag would weigh 185 grams.
maths.explain: 180 and 5 make 185 grams at the start. 185 take away 183 is 2, so 2 grams of carbon dioxide floated away. In a sealed bag the gas cannot leave, so the weight stays at 185 grams.
maths.context: In the After the Fizz experiment, vinegar and baking soda made bubbles of carbon dioxide, which left the tumbler. These made-up numbers show the same fizz on a kitchen scale.
maths.why_maths: Adding up the weights before and after shows that the missing weight is exactly the gas. So no atoms were lost.

maths.problem: In The Self-Filling Bag challenge, half a teaspoon of baking soda and 3 tablespoons of vinegar fill a small bag. A bag four times as big needs four times as much of each. How much is that?
maths.answer: 2 teaspoons of baking soda and 12 tablespoons of vinegar.
maths.explain: Four halves make 2, so 2 teaspoons of baking soda are needed. 4 times 3 is 12, so 12 tablespoons of vinegar are needed. Both reactants must grow together, or one will run out.
maths.context: In The Self-Filling Bag challenge, a sealed bag fills with carbon dioxide from vinegar and baking soda. The right amounts make it firm without popping.
maths.why_maths: Reactants are used up in a fixed proportion. Keeping the proportion lets a recipe be scaled to any size.

maths.problem: The table shows made-up results from the Rust Uses Up Air experiment. Between which two days did the water climb most? Why might it climb less each day, and then stop?
maths.answer: It climbed most between day 1 and day 2. Less oxygen was left each day, so the rusting slowed, and it stopped when the oxygen had gone.
maths.explain: From day 1 to day 2 the water climbed 1.2 centimetres. From day 2 to day 3 it climbed 0.6, then 0.2, then nothing. At the start the glass held plenty of oxygen, so the iron rusted fast. As the oxygen was used, there was less to react.

how_we_found_out.story: For about two thousand years, many people believed that the right reaction could turn lead into gold. They were called alchemists, and they worked in Egypt, China, India, the Arab world and Europe. One of the earliest we know of was a woman called Mary the Jewess. She worked in Egypt more than 1,700 years ago. She is credited with inventing the gentle water bath that cooks still use. Alchemists found real things, such as strong acids and better ways to purify substances. But nobody ever made gold. In 1661 Robert Boyle wrote that an element is a substance that cannot be broken into simpler ones. In 1789 Antoine Lavoisier in France listed 33 substances that he thought were simple. Gold and lead were both on his list. The drawings in his book were made by his wife, the chemist Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier. In 1808 John Dalton, a teacher in Manchester, explained why gold could not be made. Each element has its own kind of atom. A reaction only moves atoms into new groups. So lead atoms stay lead atoms, whatever they are mixed with.
how_we_found_out.who: The alchemists, including Mary the Jewess. Then Robert Boyle, Antoine Lavoisier and Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier, and John Dalton.
how_we_found_out.when: Alchemy lasted from about 2,000 years ago until the 1700s. Boyle wrote in 1661, Lavoisier in 1789 and Dalton in 1808.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That a chemical reaction can turn one metal into another, such as lead into gold. Two thousand years of failed attempts counted against it. Dalton then showed why. A reaction rearranges atoms, and it cannot change one kind of atom into another.
how_we_found_out.art: An old workshop with clay pots, a glass flask on a small furnace and a woman in ancient Egyptian dress lifting a pot out of a pan of hot water.

roots.context: In this unit you tested the powder left after a fizz, and watched steel wool rust inside a glass. Here we ask where the properties of a new substance come from.

deep_truth.truth: In After the Fizz, vinegar and baking soda left a new powder that no longer fizzed. In Rust Uses Up Air, hard grey steel and a gas from the air made brown crumbs. Each new substance behaved unlike both of the substances that made it. So to know what a new substance does, you have to test the substance itself.
deep_truth.habit: We expect a thing made from parts to be like its parts. A drink of lime juice and sugar is sour and sweet. In a chemical reaction this habit fails, because the product can behave unlike every reactant.
deep_truth.evidence: In After the Fizz, the crust left by vinegar and baking soda did not fizz in vinegar. Baking soda always does. In Rust Uses Up Air, steel and oxygen made rust, which is brown and crumbly. Sodium burns in water and chlorine is a poisonous gas, yet together they make table salt.

three.who_am_i: Your body is made of food, water and air that have reacted together. You run, grow and mend your own cuts. A plate of rice and a glass of water do none of these.
three.what_is_life: A living body is thousands of reactions kept going at once. In your cells, oxygen reacts with food, much as oxygen reacts with iron. Your body does it in small, careful steps.
three.what_is_this_world: Nature has only about 90 kinds of atoms. The sea, a mango, a steel bridge and you are these same atoms, joined in different ways.

roots.thread: A few kinds of atoms make millions of different substances, because joining gives properties that were not seen before. Hydrogen and oxygen are both gases, and joined together they are water. Many sages taught that one source appears as the many things of the world. Chemistry shows a small part of that picture which anyone can test. Everything is conscious, down to the atoms. How the awareness of atoms joins into the awareness of a whole body is a question nobody has answered.

teachings.source: Milindapanha (The Questions of King Milinda), Book 2, chapter 1: the chariot
teachings.teaching: The monk Nagasena asks King Milinda where his chariot is. Is it the wheels, the axle, the pole or the seat? It is none of these. 'Chariot' is the name for all the parts when they are put together.
teachings.link: Nagasena was speaking about the self, and not about chemistry. Yet rust is like his chariot. Rust is not found in iron, in oxygen or in water. It exists only when they are joined.

teachings.source: John Stuart Mill, A System of Logic (1843), Book 3, chapter 6
teachings.teaching: Mill pointed out that water has none of the properties of hydrogen or of oxygen. He said that what chemical joining produces cannot be found by adding up what each part does alone.
teachings.link: This is what the After the Fizz experiment showed. The new crust did not do what baking soda does. It had to be tested as a substance in its own right.

science.text: Since the 1920s, physicists have been able to explain why atoms join, using quantum physics. For small molecules, computers can now calculate properties such as colour before anyone makes the substance.

Whether everything about a whole can be worked out from its parts is still argued. In 1972 the physicist Philip Anderson wrote an essay called 'More Is Different'. He argued that each level of size needs laws of its own.
Philosophers who hold that awareness is in all matter face the 'combination problem'. Nobody has yet explained how many small awarenesses could join into one, as in a person.

other_view.who: The Charvaka thinkers of ancient India, as later writers describe them
other_view.view: The Charvakas said that awareness is itself a new property of this kind. Betel leaf, areca nut and lime are not red, yet chewed together they turn red. In the same way, they said, awareness appears when the elements join in a body. It ends when the body ends. Most scientists who study the brain today hold a similar view.

practice.title: The warm reaction
practice.say: Sit still and put one hand flat on your chest. Breathe in slowly. The oxygen in that breath is going to your cells. There it reacts with the food you ate today. playtest: This unit was read through step by step, as a parent and child in a city flat would use it. It has not yet been done at home. Six Mixes, Five Signs (core) uses lime juice, baking soda, salt, black tea and warm milk. Mix 1 fizzes, the tea with lime juice turns clearly paler, and warm milk makes lumps within a minute. Cold milk is slow, so the step asks for warm milk. After the Fizz (core) needs a grown-up at the stove for about 8 minutes. Open a window, because hot vinegar smells sharp. The pans must be cool before the drop test, or any liquid will sizzle. The expected result is that the water crust fizzes and the vinegar crust does not. If the vinegar crust fizzes a little, too little vinegar was used, and step 3 guards against this. Heating can turn part of the dried baking soda into washing soda. Washing soda also fizzes, so the result is the same. Drying under a fan avoids the stove, and takes a day or two. Atom Swap and Reaction Families need only coins, seeds, paper and scissors. Rust Uses Up Air needs the iron kind of steel wool, from a hardware or paint shop. Stainless steel kitchen scrubbers do not rust. With steel wool cleaned in vinegar, the water usually starts to climb within a day. It stops at about one fifth of the air space by the second or third day. The plates must be topped up so that the rims stay under water. Cold Fizz uses a whole cup of vinegar. The fizz tumbler is usually 3 to 5 degrees cooler, which most hands can tell. Some children will not notice, and the step says to record that honestly. The Self-Filling Bag is messy when a zip pops, so it is done over a tray or in the sink. The amounts given suit a pouch of about 15 by 20 centimetres and ordinary vinegar. Stronger or weaker vinegar shifts them a little. No part needs a garden, and no flame is used except the stove in After the Fizz. Nobody tastes anything. Facts to treat with care: Mary the Jewess is known only from later writers, and her dates are uncertain. Lavoisier's list of 33 simple substances included a few that are not elements. The gold made from bismuth around 1980 was far too little to see. The Charvaka view is known only from writers who disagreed with it. The story's lamp test is real, but it is not a safety rule, and the story note says so. The three videos have no address yet.
